title: Method for Detecting and Grading Cumulative Internode Length of Tomato Seedlings
author: Jin, Xin
materials: During the seedling grading process, seedlings with uniform growth and clear, easily distinguishable features are more conducive to accurate identification. However, due to various factors such as the environment and genetic material, even seedlings grown in the same environment and batch often fail to achieve uniform growth. Common issues include curved branches and leaves, as well as obscured nodes and internodes, which directly impact the effectiveness of grading and subsequent fruit growth; Additionally, cumulative internode length is embedded within the main stem, requiring precise segmentation based on the similar characteristics of the main stem and branches. Furthermore, nodes—being minute features—must be effectively predicted and identified in cluttered and obstructed environments. These issues pose significant challenges to the task of grading seedlings based on cumulative internode length. The real challenges and technical difficulties mentioned above are visualized in Figure 1.
Schematic diagram of SIoU loss function.

steps.title: Prepare tomato seedlings
steps.instruction: Select Millennium‑variety tomato seedlings grown at Chengyan Seedling Base (Luoyang, Henan). Use seedlings from a single batch that are 30–35 days old, have stem diameters of 2.8–3.5 mm, possess 4–6 main‑stem nodes, and are planted in 72‑cell trays measuring 540 mm × 280 mm.

steps.title: Manually measure cumulative internode length
steps.instruction: Using a GREENER digital vernier caliper (accuracy 0.01 mm), measure the distance from the lowest cotyledon node to the highest growth point on the main stem (sum of all internodes a‑b‑c‑d). Record each seedling’s cumulative length for later comparison with algorithm results.

steps.title: Capture seedling images
steps.instruction: Set up a simulated greenhouse environment (as shown in Figure 3A) and photograph each seedling with an Aoni C96 camera at a resolution of 3840 × 2160 pixels. Collect a total of 1 286 valid images; allocate 1 100 images for training/augmentation and 186 images for validation and error analysis.

steps.title: Annotate images with LabelMe
steps.instruction: Import the raw photos into the LabelMe annotation tool and create polygon masks. Assign label 0 to branches and leaves, label 1 to the cumulative internode‑length region, and label 2 to the cotyledon node and all tissue below it. When an internode is occluded, annotate only the visible portion.

steps.title: Augment the dataset
steps.instruction: Apply data‑augmentation operations to the 1 100 training images:

substeps.instruction: RandomBrightness with a brightness variation of ±20 % to simulate different lighting conditions.
GaussNoise with a standard deviation of 5–25 to add realistic noise.
GaussianBlur using a 3 × 3 kernel and a standard deviation of 0.1–2.0 to mimic out‑of‑focus images.
Randomly select any two of the four augmentation techniques for each image, thereby tripling the dataset to 3 300 samples.

steps.title: Configure DSH_YOLO model
steps.instruction: Build the detection network on the YOLOv8‑seg framework with three key modifications:

substeps.instruction: Insert multiple Deformable Convolution (DConv) layers into the backbone to allow adaptive sampling of curved stems and non‑rigid internodes.

Replace the original CIoU bounding‑box loss with SIoU loss, including the angle‑cost term that penalises mis‑alignment between predicted boxes and the stem axis (Λ penalty minimized at angles ≈0° or 90°, maximized near 45°).

Embed a Haar Wavelet Downsampling (HWD) module in the CSPDarknet backbone to decompose feature maps into low‑frequency (A) and high‑frequency (H, V, D) components, preserving high‑frequency stem‑edge detail while reducing spatial resolution.

steps.title: Train the model
steps.instruction: Train the DSH_YOLO network on the 3 300‑sample augmented dataset using standard YOLOv8‑seg training settings (learning rate, epochs, batch size as defined in the original code base). Keep all other YOLOv8‑seg components unchanged.

steps.title: Detect and grade seedlings
steps.instruction: Run the trained DSH_YOLO model on the 186 validation images to predict cumulative internode lengths. Compare predicted lengths with the manual measurements recorded in step 2 to assess measurement error. Classify each seedling into grades according to the non‑equidistant grading criteria defined by agronomic experts (Table 1): Grade I and Grade II for acceptable quality, other grades for over‑ or under‑grown seedlings.
